# How Bodhidharma found its canonical form

The ASCII form *bodhidharma* is not missing anything ​that this name requires. **Bodhidharma** is the canonical spelling supported by the Chinese characters evidence and the tradition's scholarly conventions. This post explains what that form preserves, how it ‌is pronounced, which narratives surround it, and why consistency matters. There are no recovered accents to celebrate; there is something more useful — a spelling whose history can actually be ‌checked.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Bodhidharma
- **ASCII form:** bodhidharma
- **Meaning:** "Dharma of awakening"
- **Domain of influence:** Zen Patriarch, Wall-Gazer
- **Pantheon:** Chinese
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form
- **Original script:** 菩提達磨 (Chinese ​characters)

## Overview

**Bodhidharma** (*bodhidharma*) — The Dharma of Awakening, First Patriarch · Dharma of awakening — belongs to the Chinese tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Zen ​Patriarch, Wall-Gazer". The name means "Dharma of awakening".

**Bodhidharma** is the First Patriarch of Zen: the Indian prince-turned-monk who crossed the Pamirs to China around 520 CE, sat facing ​a wall at Shaolin for nine years, and transmitted the Buddha’s wordless teaching outside the scriptures. His legend is the bridge between India and East Asia — and the ​seed of martial, meditative, and cultural traditions that span the continent.

PuniCodex records the canonical scholarly spelling **Bodhidharma** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/bodhidharma/). The displayed form is ASCII-equivalent ​— a description computed from the displayed form itself. The plain ASCII form *bodhidharma* contains the same letters: no recovered diacritics or special encoding is claimed. The work here ‌is consistent citation, capitalization, provenance, and cultural context.

## The Name

The name is attested in Chinese characters as **菩提達磨**. Etymologically it means "Dharma of awakening".

The canonical spelling **Bodhidharma** ​matches the conventional scholarly romanization. ## ‌The Original Script

The name is written in Chinese characters as **菩提達磨**. That attested script remains the primary evidence for the conventional romanization **Bodhidharma**. The canonical Latin spelling does ​not pretend to recover marks it never contained: it fixes one reviewed reference form while leaving the original script visible for comparison.

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is ‌**/ˌboʊdɪˈdɑːrmə/** — Sanskrit → Chinese transmission (Pútídámó).

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Bodhi-** — From Sanskrit bodhi, “awakening” — the name begins in the Buddha’s own enlightenment-word.
- **-dhar-** — From √dhṛ, ​“to hold, sustain” — the same root as dharma’s “that which holds”.
- **-ma** — The Chinese rendered it 菩提達磨 (Pútídámó); the Japanese, Daruma; the West, Bodhidharma.

For the modern ​speaker, the closest approximation is: “boh-dee-DAR-muh”

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Chinese** — Pútídámó 菩提達磨 — the First Patriarch
- **Japanese** — Daruma 達磨 — the roly-poly doll ​is his image

The name means “awakening-perfection” or “dharma of awakening” — the Indian prince who carried Zen to China.

## Mythology

Bodhidharma’s mythology is a layer-cake of history and ​legend: the historical missionary of the early sixth century; the wall-gazer of the Zen records; the Shaolin temple’s patron of the martial arts; and Japan’s round Daruma doll, whose blank ​eyes you fill in when your wish comes true. The legend grew because the teaching needed a body — and the body it chose was defiant, foreign, and perfectly ‌still.

### The Crossing to China (Transmission Records)

The Zen records send him to the court of the Liang emperor Wudi — the great Buddhist patron who asks, ‘what is ​the highest meaning of the holy truth?’ and is told ‘vast emptiness, nothing holy’. The emperor, scandalized, asks who stands before him: ‘Don’t know’, says the future patriarch, and ‌leaves for the north. The dialogue founded the Zen interview-style in a single exchange.

### Nine Years, One Wall (Wall-Gazing Legend)

At Shaolin he sat facing a wall nine years; legend ​adds that in frustration at sleep he cut off his eyelids — and tea, the meditator’s ally, sprang from where they fell. Huike, his future successor, stood in the ‌snow and cut off his own arm to prove his sincerity; Bodhidharma accepted him and transmitted the teaching. The tradition’s founding images are all of this order: resolve measured ​in what one will lose.

### The Temple and the Arts (Shaolin Cycle)

The legend that he taught the Shaolin monks exercises to strengthen their meditation — the seed of ‌Shaolin kung fu — belongs to the later layers, but it fixed his place in the martial imagination: the first patriarch as the first master of body-discipline. The *Yi ​Jin Jing* muscle-classic attaches itself to his name.

### The Round Wish-Keeper (Daruma Doll)

Japan made him a doll: round as the wall-sitter’s robe, weighted to right itself — *nanakorobi yaoki*, ‌fall seven times, rise eight. You paint one blank eye when you make a wish, the other when it comes true. The fierce Indian master ended as Japan’s most ​cheerful household god of perseverance, keeping his scowl and his self-righting bottom.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Bodhidharma concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each ​a compressed statement about the name:

- **The Wall-Gazing** — Nine years facing the wall at Shaolin; the tradition’s image of unmoving resolve — and of the mind’s own wall.
- ‌**The First Patriarch** — The twenty-eighth Indian patriarch who became China’s first — the wordless transmission passed through him.
- **Daruma’s Eyes** — The legend: he cut off his eyelids in ‌wrath at sleep — and where they fell, tea plants grew. Japan’s doll watches with one eye.
- **The Bone of the Buddha** — His only transmission: a bowl, a ‌robe, and a bone — the mind-to-mind seal outside the scriptures.

## Archaeology & Evidence

The material record for Bodhidharma survives in a small number of securely identified remains, catalogued ​below; the corpus is thin but unambiguous, and each site is tied to the name by ancient testimony.

His supposed grave at Kongxiangsi in the Pagoda Forest of Shaolin ​carries the earliest memorials; the Shaolin steles of the Tang dynasty name him. The Daruma doll’s manufacture is a modern industry, but the blank-eyed scowl descends from the Muromachi portraits.

## ‌Realm & Domain

**Bodhidharma** is the First Patriarch of Zen: the Indian prince-turned-monk who crossed the Pamirs to China around 520 CE, sat facing a wall at Shaolin for ​nine years, and transmitted the Buddha’s wordless teaching outside the scriptures. His legend is the bridge between India and East Asia — and the seed of martial, meditative, and ​cultural traditions that span the continent.

### The Wall-Gazing

Nine years facing the wall at Shaolin; the tradition’s image of unmoving resolve — and of the mind’s own wall.

### The ‌First Patriarch

The twenty-eighth Indian patriarch who became China’s first — the wordless transmission passed through him.

### Daruma’s Eyes

The legend: he cut off his eyelids in wrath at ​sleep — and where they fell, tea plants grew. Japan’s doll watches with one eye.

### The Bone of the Buddha

His only transmission: a bowl, a robe, and a bone ​— the mind-to-mind seal outside the scriptures.

## Across Cultures

Bodhidharma is the Silk Road made flesh: Indian dharma, Chinese wall, Japanese doll. The Zen lineages count him as the ‌twenty-eighth Indian and first Chinese patriarch — the hinge of the transmission; and the Tibetan traditions remember him (as Bodhidharmottara) among the great siddhas. His defiance of the Liang ​emperor became the template of the Zen master’s whole pedagogy.

Within the Chinese tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[bagua|Bāguà]], [[caishen|Cáishén]], [[change|Chángé]], [[fuxi|Fúxī]], [[guandi|Guāndì]], and [[guanyin|Guānyīn]].

## Cultural ‌Legacy

He stands at the head of every Zen lineage — Rinzai and Sōtō alike trace the wall; the Shaolin temple’s global fame rests on his legend; and the Daruma ​doll, with its self-righting scowl, is Japan’s most reproduced folk object. ‘Zen’ as the West knows it begins, by the tradition’s own account, with his ‘don’t know’.

## A Meditation

Bodhidharma: the name is a doctrine — awakening-holding, the dharma that holds itself awake. Restored plainly, it spans ‌the journey it names: an Indian word, a Chinese wall, a Japanese doll, and the plain letters any reader can hold. Five syllables, one transmission.
